claims.section: Overview: Galaxy Evolution as a Regulated Baryon Cycle
claims.text: Galaxy quenching is jointly regulated by internal mass-linked processes and environment-linked processes; the separability and relative priority of those channels depend on sample selection, redshift, and how quenching is measured.

Gas removal and depletion can suppress star formation by reducing the usable cold-gas reservoir, but the evidence should distinguish true reservoir loss from morphological quenching, turbulent regulation, and environment-specific stripping.

Satellite galaxies can experience environmental quenching after infall into groups or clusters, especially when simulations or observations identify quenched low-mass systems as satellite analogues rather than isolated centrals.

Galaxy environment correlates with morphology and colour, but alignment or morphology-only evidence should be treated as contextual unless it directly connects dense environments to quenched early-type populations.
Environmental quenching signatures at high redshift are plausible but should be presented as an active observational constraint, not as a settled universal pathway.
Dense groups and clusters can accelerate transformation through hydrodynamical interaction with the intracluster medium and gravitational processing, but the dominant channel is system-dependent.
Cosmic-web filaments, sheets, nodes, and voids can shape galaxy evolution through coherent tidal fields that torque protogalactic gas and influence later accretion geometry.
AGN or SMBH feedback is a real but scoped quenching pathway in galaxy evolution, not a universal explanation for why galaxies stop forming stars.

AGN activity can drive molecular, ionized, or neutral gas outflows capable of removing or depleting star-forming fuel in selected massive or AGN-host galaxies, with detection rates remaining tracer- and sample-dependent.

AGN feedback is one quenching axis among several; central/bulge/black-hole predictors, halo/environment/satellite pathways, strangulation, stripping, gas retention, low star-formation efficiency, and star-formation-driven outflows remain alternatives or qualifiers.

Gas-reservoir language requires caution: central-kiloparsec depletion can occur in some AGN hosts, while other quenched systems retain large gas reservoirs or show low star-formation efficiency, so gas removal alone cannot explain every quenching pathway.

Preventive or maintenance feedback is distinct from ejective outflows; current maintenance/heating support in this source set remains model-dependent or simulation-bounded rather than a measured prevalence result.

Kinetic/radio-mode AGN feedback can mechanically couple jets or outflows to surrounding gas and inject kinetic or thermal energy in radio galaxies, galaxy groups/clusters, and simulations, but current evidence supports a context-dependent mechanism rather than a population-wide quenching channel.

In selected massive galaxies at cosmic noon (roughly z≈1.5–3), star formation can shut down rapidly, with AGN activity or AGN feedback implicated in some observations and simulations; this remains a sample- and model-dependent pathway rather than a universal z∼2 quenching rule.
